new_entities.name: Gastrointestinal bleeding risk
new_entities.description: Risk of clinically important upper gastrointestinal bleeding or hemorrhage.

edges.effect_quant: The clearest quantitative signal is not subtle: the classic hospital case-control study found odds ratios of 4.9 to 19.1 for individual non-aspirin NSAIDs, and the large multicenter genotype-stratified case-control study still found odds ratios above 4 among exposed users.
edges.population: adults using non-aspirin NSAIDs for recurrent or chronic analgesic or anti-inflammatory treatment
edges.mechanism: Chronic NSAID exposure impairs cyclooxygenase-dependent prostaglandin protection in the gastroduodenal mucosa, making bleeding more likely when mucosal injury, erosions, or ulcers occur.
edges.summary: This is one of the least ambiguous iatrogenic edges in the graph. Across classic case-control work and later randomized-trial meta-analysis, chronic or repeated NSAID exposure consistently increases the risk of serious upper gastrointestinal bleeding complications, with the largest harms seen for higher-risk individual agents rather than a perfectly uniform class effect.
edges.caveats: Magnitude varies by molecule, dose, age, ulcer history, and co-medications such as aspirin or anticoagulants. The strongest quantitative papers focus on upper GI hemorrhage or composite upper GI complications rather than every possible lower-GI bleed phenotype.
